name: Yeonji rouge for lips and cheeks

lead: Yeonji is the Korean word for rouge, a red colour applied to the lips and cheeks in traditional Korean makeup. It adds colour and a healthy-looking flush to the face.

Rouge could be made from safflower, a plant long used in East Asian cosmetics. Historical accounts place Korean cosmetics in the Three Kingdoms and Goryeo periods, and describe plant-based products. No clinical studies exist on yeonji.

paras: Traditionally the colour was dabbed onto the lips and cheeks. Modern users interested in the look typically choose red or rose lip and cheek products in a similar soft flush.
Safflower-based colour is a plant pigment, but some historic rouges elsewhere used cinnabar and red lead, which are toxic. Allergic reactions to any cosmetic ingredient are possible.

chain: Apply red rouge to lips and cheeks
angle.text: Yeonji adds a red tint to the lips and cheeks, which brightens the face. The effect is visible immediately while worn.

lead: Yeonji is the Korean name for rouge, used to colour the lips and cheeks.[1] Its look is a red flush on the lips and cheeks that brightens the face.

Korean cosmetics date to the Three Kingdoms period and flourished under Goryeo, with early products made from plants; safflower provided oils for skin and could also be made into rouge.[1] In the Joseon period, Confucian values discouraged lavish makeup, though upper-class women often copied the style of gisaeng entertainers.[1]

Rouge is an old cosmetic across cultures: in China it dates to the Shang dynasty and was made from safflower juice, and in Rome it used red lead and cinnabar, a mixture linked to illness and death.[2] No clinical studies on yeonji have been found.
infobox: Cosmetics from Three Kingdoms and Goryeo onward

paras: Yeonji coloured the lips and cheeks.[1] Traditional Korean makeup also emphasised eyebrows, drawn with plant-ash ink in black, blue or dark brown, with crescent and willow-leaf shapes the most favoured.[1]

Early Korean cosmetics included lotions from gourd stems, ground mung bean for cleansing and camellia oil for hair; safflower oil moistened skin and gave sheen.[1] After the 1876 Treaty of Kanghwa opened Korean ports, Western styles gained influence, and Bakgabun, the first mass-produced Korean face powder, sold strongly from 1916 to 1930 until its lead content hurt sales.[1]
Rouge was used in ancient Egypt from fat and red ochre, in Greece from crushed berries and beet juice, and in China from safflower.[2] Modern rouge may use carmine.[2]

timeline.event: Treaty of Kanghwa opens Korean ports; Western cosmetics gain influence.[1]
